meta.title: A Message for America’s Students
meta.speaker: Barack Obama
meta.occasion: National address to schoolchildren, Wakefield High School, Arlington VA, 8 September 2009
meta.blurb: A "here is how to be a student" address actually addressed to students.
meta.credit: Barack Obama, "A Message for America’s Students," 8 September 2009. The White House. Public domain (work of the U.S. Government).

summary.text:
Obama's first back-to-school address, delivered at Wakefield High School and broadcast to classrooms nationwide. The thesis lands early: the best teachers, parents and schools in the world make no difference unless students fulfill their own responsibilities [1].

Education is framed two ways. First as self-discovery — every student is good at something, and school is where you find out what [2]. Then as a national stake: quitting on school is quitting on your country [3].

The middle is personal: lessons from his mother at 4:30 in the morning [4], a father who left when he was two, and the second chances that followed [5]. The close reframes failure as method — you have to let your failures teach you — and ends on a question addressed to each listener: what's your contribution going to be [6]?

citations.quote: none of it will make a difference -- none of it will matter -- unless all of you fulfill your responsibilities.
Every single one of you has something that you're good at. Every single one of you has something to offer. And you have a responsibility to yourself to discover what that is.
if you quit on school, you're not just quitting on yourself, you're quitting on your country.
But because she had to go to work, the only time she could do it was at 4:30 in the morning.
I got a lot of second chances, and I had the opportunity to go to college and law school and follow my dreams.
What's your contribution going to be? What problems are you going to solve? What discoveries will you make?

at.quote: I am here with students at Wakefield High School in Arlington, Virginia.
Now, I know that for many of you, today is the first day of school.
When I was young, my family lived overseas. I lived in Indonesia for a few years.
I want to start with the responsibility you have to yourself.
Where you are right now doesn't have to determine where you'll end up. No one has written your destiny for you.
I'm calling on each of you to set your own goals for your education
Some of the most successful people in the world are the ones who've had the most failures.
So today, I want to ask all of you: What's your contribution going to be?

concepts.definition: The speech's organizing word, deliberately turned around: after teachers', parents' and government's responsibilities comes the one the speech exists for — the student's own.

cite.quote: I've given a lot of speeches about education, and I've talked about responsibility a lot.

concepts.definition: The autobiographical warrant: trouble and drift at school didn't have to be destiny, because chances to recover existed — the speech asks students to use theirs earlier.

cite.quote: I got a lot of second chances, and I had the opportunity to go to college and law school and follow my dreams.

concepts.definition: The closing argument against perfectionism: Rowling's rejections and Jordan's missed shots as evidence that failures instruct rather than define.

cite.quote: You have to let them show you what to do differently the next time.

flags.text: The one explicit ask: set your own goals for your education, and commit.

cite.quote: I'm calling on each of you to set your own goals for your education

flags.text: The seasonal PSA: wash your hands, stay home when sick.

cite.quote: I hope all of you are washing your hands a lot, and that you stay home from school when you don't feel well

notes.text: "Buster" — the most human moment in the speech; the mother at the kitchen table is the whole argument.
notes.quote: "This is no picnic for me either, Buster."

notes.text: if you quit on school, you're not just quitting on yourself, you're quitting on your country.

notes.text: Don't be afraid to ask for help when you need it. I do that every day. Asking for help isn't a sign of weakness. It's a sign of strength.
